transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-05
Start: 14:00 PT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: yes
Attendees: Marisa Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Jordan Miles (Atlas - Head of ML), Priya Singh (Atlas - Platform Eng), Oliver Grant (Atlas - CTO)

Summary: Quick Optimize walkthrough focused on batching and prefix/KV cache recommendations for Atlas Financial's customer-facing chat flows. Discussed tradeoffs (latency vs cost), example cost model for 1M requests, and next steps to run a short benchmark using Atlas sample traces. Customer asked about VPC/on-prem options, KMS encryption, and how caching interacts with PII retention policies.

[00:00] Marisa: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros? I'll start — Marisa Chen, AE at Redwood.
[00:10] Jordan: Jordan Miles, Head of ML at Atlas. we've got Priya and Oliver here as well.
[00:15] Priya: hi, Priya Singh, platform eng.
[00:18] Oliver: Oliver Grant, CTO.
[00:20] Diego: Diego Ramos, solutions engineer on Optimize and runtime perf — I'll drive the demo.

[00:30] Marisa: Cool. objective for today: Diego will walk through Redwood Optimize recommendations around batching and the prefix/KV cache, show a cost model, and we'll align on what Atlas needs for a short POC.
[00:45] Diego: Great. high level first — we see two levers that move cost: batching at the request layer, and prefix or KV caching which reuses token generation for repeated prefixes. Both can reduce per-token cost substantially but you trade off latency and cache hit characteristics.

[01:20] Diego: Quick note — I'm going to reference the Optimize console and our cost spreadsheet. I have an example workload that resembles a financial chat: lots of short prompts (20-80 tokens) with a handful of longer context windows for account history.
[01:40] Jordan: that's accurate. about 70% of our calls are short Q/A style, 25% are multi-turn account summaries, and 5% are long batch reports.

[02:05] Diego: Ok, so batching — two types: request-side batching (collecting requests into a single GPU batch) and token-level batching inside the runtime. request-side batching increases throughput and lowers per-token compute but increases tail latency. For your SLA — you said 250ms p95 for critical flows?
[02:25] Priya: Correct. for account lookup we need <300ms p95; for general chat we can accept up to 1s p95.

[02:40] Diego: Good. So our recommendation: keep critical flows on lower-batch sizes or use dedicated capacity with prewarmed pools (we can pin capacity), while opportunistic flows can use higher batching to save cost. here is an example: small batch (batch_size 4, token concurrency low) yields median 120ms p50 and p95 around 260ms; larger batch (batch_size 16+) moves p95 above 450ms but reduces tokens/second cost by ~35% in this workload.

[03:30] Jordan: how does that interact with decoding? we run streaming in prod.
[03:35] Diego: streaming still works; batching mostly affects the time until the model begins generating for a given request. once generation starts, streaming tokens flow as normal. so you see a startup latency penalty.

[04:00] Diego: Now KV / prefix cache. two flavors: prefix caching (store the model KV cache for identical prefixes/prompts) and semantic caching at the response level. prefix/KV cache is best when you have repeated system prompts or repeated user scaffolding. it saves the model from recomputing attention for tokens in the prefix. in practice for your site, repeated regulatory disclaimers and standard account context are good candidates.

[04:30] Priya: curious about PII. if we cache prefix KVs that contain account identifiers, is that a compliance hazard?
[04:40] Diego: Good question. you can control cache keys; Redwood Optimize supports redaction and hash-only keys. we recommend hashing user identifiers and storing only non-PII in the cache key. for sensitive contexts we support TTLs and configurable per-route cache policies. also with Private deployments (VPC/on-prem) you control storage location and can use your KMS.

[05:10] Oliver: about KMS — do you integrate with our cloud KMS? we have AWS KMS and an HSM for certain keys.
[05:16] Diego: Yes — Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS integrations. we can configure envelope encryption with your KMS or use a hardware-backed HSM for critical keys. we'll send our KMS integration doc.

[05:35] Jordan: what's the realistic hit-rate for KV cache on a financial chat product?
[05:40] Diego: depends on prompt variance. for our customers with templated prompts we often see 20-40% hit rates on prefixes, sometimes higher for flows with repetitive system prompts. for account-context where a chunk of the prompt is unique per-user, hit rate can be lower unless you split static vs dynamic prefixes.

[06:10] Diego: Example cost model — I pulled numbers from our catalog. baseline hosted model on gpus (open-7b style): cost X per 1M tokens. with batching and a 30% KV hit rate, you can see effective token compute drop by ~28-38% depending on batch configuration. I shared a sheet in the chat (link) — it's the "Optimize cost delta by batch + KV" file.

[06:45] Priya: can you show the sheet and an example scenario?
[06:50] Diego: Yep — (screen) scenario A: 1M short requests (avg 50 tokens) all hosted, no caching, small batch = baseline cost $3,400 (example number). Scenario B: add batching to moderate levels + 30% KV hits = effective cost $2,200 — that's ~35% savings. Scenario C: Dedicated capacity (reserved) with aggressive batching + quantized model variant gets you to $1,500. numbers are illustrative — we'll run your traces to get precise.

[07:30] Jordan: those numbers look good. what about quality regression when switching quantized model?
[07:35] Diego: we recommend running A/B evals. Redwood Optimize has eval hooks: you can pin a model, run canary traffic, and monitor quality metrics on a prompt set. quantization to int8 or Q4 can slightly affect generation on edge cases; our team provides recommended profiles per model and per workload.

[08:05] Diego: Also note cache invalidation and rollouts — if you change system prompt you should invalidate relevant keys. we support scoped invalidation and time-based TTL.

[08:25] Priya: operationally, where is the cache stored for hosted? is it in your infra?
[08:30] Diego: Hosted stores cache in our managed store (encrypted at rest). for Private deployments you can put cache in your VPC-backed store or S3-compatible store, and again you control encryption keys.

[08:50] Oliver: latency impact of cache reads?
[08:55] Diego: Cache reads are an in-memory lookup on the serving node in the dedicated case — sub-ms. In hosted with remote cache store the lookup can add ~5-12ms depending on region and store. still much cheaper than recomputing the prefix several tokens.

[09:20] Diego: quick demo — I'll switch to the Optimize console. (screenshare) here's the per-route config, batching profile, and cache policy. you can define route-level batching windows, max batch size, and per-route TTL. you can also set a policy to always bypass cache for routes tagged "PII".

[10:00] Diego: For example, we have a route called "account-summary" where we set batching window = 30ms, max batch size = 8, prefix cache TTL = 15 minutes, and key pattern that strips user_id. that combo in our tests gave a 24% cost reduction and kept p95 under 300ms.

[10:30] Priya: how do we reproduce this in our environment? do you need data?
[10:34] Diego: We'll need sample traces: prompt lengths, frequency, p95 targets. ideally a couple hours of real traffic or a representative replay. Priya: can you share traces?
[10:45] Priya: yes, we can extract anonymized traces and upload to the S3 link you provide.

[11:00] Diego: Great. Next I want to show how batching interacts with autoscaling. If you use Redwood Dedicated you can configure prewarmed pools and burst capacity. prewarmed nodes reduce cold-start tail latency so you can safely increase batch sizes.

[11:30] Jordan: what's the SLA for Dedicated?
[11:33] Marisa: For Dedicated we have an SLA tier with 99.9% uptime and latency objectives tailored per contract. we'll send the SLA pdf.

[11:45] Diego: Another practical tip: split static system context (policy, disclaimers) into a static prefix and dynamic user context. Cache the static prefix and only send the dynamic portion. That increases hit-rate without exposing PII.

[12:05] Priya: for our multi-tenant product is there a danger of cache poisoning?

[12:09] Diego: No, caches are scoped per-customer and per-route. keys include tenant context and are hashed. we also provide rate limiting and monitoring per key.

[12:30] Diego: I'll now walk through the cost model cli/console export for your traffic. (screen) we can run a synthetic replay or real replay — we recommend real replay. for the synthetic snapshot I used: 1M requests with the distribution Jordan described.

[13:00] Diego: When we run your trace in the benchmark harness we produce: latency histogram, cache hit/miss breakdown, token throughput, and an estimated monthly cost under hosted vs dedicated. Diego: note — the cost estimate includes compute but excludes egress and some infra fees; we'll call those out in the spreadsheet.

[13:35] Jordan: can we get an estimate for 10M requests/month?

[13:40] Diego: yes — once we have the traces we'll scale the model. ballpark: if 1M = $3.4k baseline, 10M scales roughly linearly but batching efficiencies can improve marginal cost — so 10M might be 9x baseline or slightly less. dedicated commitments materially change that curve.

[14:05] Priya: security questions: SOC 2 and audit logs — do you provide end-to-end audit logs for inference?

[14:12] Marisa: We provide per-request audit logs, data residency options, SSO/SAML, and role-based access. SOC 2 Type II report is available — we'll share the cert and the security pack.

[14:30] Oliver: legal will want to see data retention controls.

[14:33] Marisa: we have TTL controls on logs and caching and can configure retention windows per customer contract.

[14:45] Diego: back to performance — here's a deeper slide: token-level batching and prompt parallelism options. for multi-turn chats you can cache KV for the static preamble, then stream tokens generated from dynamic context. this saves compute for the repeated attention layers.

[15:10] Priya: what's the engineering lift to integrate the SDK? we use Node + Go in prod.

[15:16] Diego: Redwood has SDKs for Node, Python, Go. integration is a few endpoints: call the /generate route with route config and cache flags. we can share a starter repo. expected engineering effort for a basic integration is 2-4 days. for a full POC with trace replay and benchmarks probably 1-2 sprints.

[15:45] Jordan: ok, timeline — we'd like a 2-week POC starting mid-November.

[15:50] Marisa: sounds doable — if Priya can share traces by 11/12 we can run benchmarks week of 11/16 and present results 11/20.

[16:05] Diego: wrapping up with risks: batching may affect cold-start p95; quantization can affect quality on corner cases. we'll run A/B tests and show delta metrics.

[16:25] Jordan: noted. anything else on cost breakdown?

[16:28] Diego: one more item — caching granularity. we typically recommend TTLs 5-20 minutes for prefix caches in chat to balance freshness vs savings for financial disclaimers and session state.

[16:45] Priya: curious about monitoring — can we see token-level cost in the console?

[16:50] Diego: yes — Optimize console exposes token-level cost, per-route latency, and cache hit ratios. you can set alerts for regressions.

[17:05] Marisa: quick check on procurement — Atlass procurement will need pricing sheet and security packet. I'll loop in our account exec and send.

[17:18] Jordan: legal will want a short-term commitment for Dedicated?

[17:22] Marisa: not necessarily; Dedicated can be contract-based, we also have burst and hybrid options if you want to start hosted and move to Dedicated as volume grows.

[17:40] Oliver: for regulatory reasons, we may prefer Private for certain flows. is there an on-prem option?

[17:45] Diego: Yes — our Private deployment can be VPC-hosted or on-prem boxed install for air-gapped. that said, it adds some ops overhead. we'll include the Private deployment whitepaper in the packet.

[18:05] Diego: final demo bit — here's an exported benchmark. (screen) I can toggle cache on/off and show delta in real-time. cache on — p95 drops 120ms and compute drops 32% at 30% hit rate. cache off — p95 moves up and cost increases.

[18:40] Priya: that's convincing. one question — can we do partial caching where we cache only the system prompt and not the conversation?

[18:45] Diego: yes — that's the recommended pattern. cache static system prompt, strip or hash dynamic user fields.

[19:00] Marisa: ok let's summarize next steps. Priya to share anonymized traces by 2026-11-12. Diego will prepare a benchmark and run it week of 11/16. Marisa will send pricing, SLA, SOC2 + KMS docs by 11/09. Jordan to confirm POC objectives by 11/10.

[19:25] Jordan: agreed. thanks everyone, this was helpful.

[19:28] Oliver: thanks.

[19:30] Diego: we'll follow up with links and schedule the benchmark kickoff.

End transcript.
